title: Ride-share legalisation (2015 to 2018)
design: Staggered: each group of states that legalised in the same year against states that had not yet (WA legalised in 2019). Method: stacked difference-in-differences, net of the same comparison for unaffected industries in the same states.
comparison: Treated: ACT, NSW, NT, QLD, SA, TAS, VIC. Comparison: NT, VIC, WA.
grade_reason: A pre-reform year lies outside its 95% placebo band.
headline: Not identified. Taxi and road-transport entry in the legalising states was already far above the comparison states in the years before legalisation, so the comparison fails its pre-reform check. Ride-sharing also ran before it was legal, and drivers had to register for GST from August 2015 wherever it ran.

category_summaries.competition: Not identified: the states diverged before legalisation, so no estimate is headlined.
category_summaries.prices: Descriptive only. Urban transport fares are mostly public transport.
category_summaries.productivity: Not measurable at division level. Shown for description only.

key_insights: The question: did legalising ride-sharing (2015 to 2018) change how many taxi and road passenger businesses started or closed?
The comparison: each group of states that legalised together against states that had not yet.
What we found: no answer is possible. Openings in the legalising states were already far above the comparison states before legalisation, so the comparison fails its pre-reform check.
Why: ride-sharing ran before it was legal in most cities, and every driver had to register for GST from August 2015, so the legal dates are not when the market changed.
What it means: a different design is needed, such as the dates ride-sharing actually arrived in each city.

method.estimand: The average change in the treated industries' entry (or exit) rate in the adopting states over the exposed years, relative to the comparison states, beyond the change for unaffected industries in the same states (ACT, NSW, NT, QLD, SA, TAS, VIC).
method.identification: Without the reform, the treated industries' rate in the adopting states would have moved as in the comparison states once state-wide changes shared with unaffected industries are removed (triple-difference parallel trends). Checked with the pre-reform event-study coefficients.
method.inference: No conventional standard errors (few treated states). p-value: two-sided rank of hat{β}^{net} among the P centred placebo estimates. 90% interval: hat{β}^{net} minus the 95th and 5th percentiles of the centred placebos (Conley and Taber 2011). Smallest detectable effect: 2.8 × their standard deviation.
steps: Took the treated industries (4623 Taxi and Other Road Transport) and the adopting states and dates from the register records; cohorts: ACT, NSW from 2015-16 to 2016-17 against VIC, NT, WA; SA, QLD, TAS in 2016-17 against VIC, NT, WA; VIC, NT in 2017-18 against WA. Comparison states are those not yet treated in each cohort's window.
Built yearly entry and exit rates from ABS Counts of Australian Businesses (registered release vintage), 2007-08 on, pooling the treated classes in each state.
Drew placebo groups of the same number of classes from outside the treated division, matched on size (14500 businesses in the treated states in 2014-15); 43 qualified.

Design stage with every treated outcome hidden: checked the feasibility rules (at least 100 treated businesses and 19 placebo groups) and the power, then committed the plan (docs/pap_high_evaluability.md).
Estimated the stacked difference-in-differences for the treated group and every placebo group, and subtracted the placebo mean.
Checked each pre-reform year against its 95% placebo band, and ran the registered robustness variants (the other ABS vintage, employing businesses only, leaving each state out).
Applied the plan's decision and grading rules, with Benjamini–Hochberg q-values across the batch.
Prices: the same estimator on each city's CPI class relative to its all-groups index, against placebo CPI classes, with a registered variant that removes each city's pre-reform linear trend.
